title: Stubbornness & Obstinacy
rule: This cluster describes refusal to change one's mind or yield to persuasion, authority, or treatment, ranging from admirably firm (steadfast, resolute) to perversely unbending (obdurate, intransigent). The GRE signals it with phrases like 'despite repeated appeals,' 'refused every overture,' or 'far from conciliatory,' and sets tone traps: a writer who admires persistence wants steadfast or pertinacious, not obstinate or headstrong.
tip: Hear the hardness in the roots: ob-DUR-ate comes from durus ('hard,' as in durable), and in-TRANS-igent is someone who will not transact a compromise.

words.m: stubbornly refusing to change one's opinion or course; hardhearted
words.s: Even after the evidence of wrongdoing became overwhelming, the obdurate official refused to apologize, insisting that his critics simply misunderstood the agency's mission.

words.m: unwilling to compromise or moderate a position
words.s: Negotiations collapsed because both delegations remained intransigent, each treating the smallest concession as an unforgivable betrayal of its constituents.
words.root: Latin in- 'not' + transigere, 'to come to terms'

words.m: stubbornly resisting authority, control, or treatment
words.s: The new principal found the faculty recalcitrant, its senior members openly ignoring every directive that threatened the routines they had followed for decades.
words.root: Latin re- 'back' + calcitrare, 'to kick' (like a mule)

words.m: unreasonably determined to keep one's opinion or course despite persuasion
words.s: Her obstinate refusal to consult a doctor, even as her symptoms worsened week after week, baffled family members who had begged her to reconsider.
words.root: Latin obstinare, 'to persist, set one's mind on'

words.m: refusing to be persuaded; utterly firm in a stated position
words.s: Although her advisers urged a softer tone, the senator was adamant that the bill pass without the amendments its opponents had demanded.
words.root: Greek adamas, 'unbreakable'; also the root of diamond

words.m: hard to control, manage, or solve; stubborn
words.s: Decades of failed reforms suggest that rural poverty in the region is an intractable problem, resistant to every remedy policymakers have yet devised.

words.m: stubbornly unmanageable; resistant to treatment, heat, or stimulus
words.s: The refractory infection persisted through three courses of antibiotics, forcing physicians to try an experimental therapy they had hoped to reserve for emergencies.

words.m: holding firmly to a purpose or opinion; persistently determined
words.s: A pertinacious investigator, she filed records requests for eleven years until the agency finally released the documents proving the contamination.

words.m: self-willed and determined to act without heeding advice
words.s: The headstrong young captain ignored the harbor master's storm warnings and set sail at dusk, convinced that caution was merely a symptom of age.
words.root: Led by one's own head rather than another's reins

words.m: deliberately and stubbornly following one's own wishes; intentional
words.s: The court ruled that the company's failure to report the leak was not an oversight but willful concealment, and it imposed the maximum penalty.
words.root: Will + -ful; British spelling 'wilful' drops one l

words.m: firmly loyal or unwavering in purpose, belief, or allegiance
words.s: Through two decades of ridicule from the scientific establishment, she remained steadfast in her conviction that continents drift, and later data vindicated her.
words.root: Old English stede 'place' + fæst 'firm': fixed in place

words.m: admirably purposeful, determined, and unwavering
words.s: Faced with a hostile board and dwindling funds, the resolute director pressed ahead with the restoration, refusing to let the museum's collection be sold piecemeal.
words.root: Latin resolutus, 'settled': a mind already made up

tc.q: Those who expected the newly elected premier to soften her party's hard line were soon disabused: far from seeking common ground, she proved even more _____ than her predecessor, rejecting every overture from the opposition.
tc.why: 'Far from seeking common ground' and 'rejecting every overture' call for refusal to compromise: intransigent. Conciliatory is the exact opposite, and capricious and ambivalent imply wavering, not a hard line.

tc.q: Although the tumor had initially responded to chemotherapy, it eventually became _____, shrinking no further no matter how the dosage or drug combination was adjusted.
tc.why: 'Although it initially responded' sets up a shift to resisting treatment, which is the medical sense of refractory. Responsive is the trap, describing the earlier state the sentence contrasts against.

tc.q: The diplomat's reputation for (i) _____ was well earned: in thirty years of negotiation she had never abandoned a position merely because it was unpopular. Yet her admirers insisted that this firmness was principled rather than (ii) _____, since she yielded readily whenever presented with new evidence.
tc.why: Never abandoning a position defines steadfastness. Her admirers then separate principled firmness from mere obduracy, and 'yielded readily to new evidence' shows she was not obdurate. Judicious is praise, so it cannot be what the admirers are denying.

tc.q: Teachers who had found the boy (i) _____ in the classroom, defying every rule and ignoring every reprimand, were astonished to learn that on the soccer field he was a model of (ii) _____, accepting his coach's every instruction without complaint.
tc.why: 'Defying every rule' glosses recalcitrant, and 'astonished' marks a reversal into its opposite, docility ('accepting every instruction'). Diffident means shy, not defiant, and truculence would repeat his classroom behavior rather than contrast with it.

se.q: Though the board had hoped the founder would gracefully accept retirement, he remained _____, vowing to fight any attempt to remove him from the company he had built.
se.why: 'Vowing to fight' any removal signals unbending refusal: adamant and obdurate. Tractable and pliant are a synonym pair that means the opposite, and ambivalent contradicts his firm vow.

se.q: The historian argues that the rebellion's leaders were not reckless but _____: having weighed the odds carefully, they persisted in their cause long after lesser figures had abandoned it.
se.why: 'Not reckless' plus 'weighed the odds carefully' requires an approving word for persistence: resolute and steadfast. Headstrong, willful, and impetuous all suggest the heedless stubbornness the historian rejects.

se.q: Attempts to reform the agency's procurement practices have been thwarted not by any single opponent but by a _____ bureaucracy that absorbs every directive without ever changing its habits.
se.why: A bureaucracy that resists every directive is recalcitrant or refractory. Pliable and malleable are a matching pair with the opposite meaning, and venal (corrupt) might describe a bureaucracy but has no partner and does not explain the resistance to change.

se.q: Far from being a liability, the patient's _____ nature proved an asset in her recovery: she persisted with grueling physical therapy long after her doctors expected her to give up.
se.why: Persisting long after others expected her to quit shows a pertinacious or tenacious nature. Capricious and mercurial form a tempting pair, but both mean changeable, the opposite of persistent.

title: Compliance & Docility
rule: This cluster covers readiness to obey, yield, or be shaped by others, from neutral openness (amenable, tractable) to reluctant surrender (acquiesce, capitulate) to spineless passivity (supine, submissive). The GRE often sets these words against the stubbornness cluster across a contrast signal, and it tests connotation: amenable can be praise, while supine and submissive usually imply weakness.
tip: Docile comes from Latin docere, 'to teach' (a docile creature is easy to teach), and tractable from trahere, 'to draw' (it is easily drawn along).

words.m: ready to accept control or instruction; submissive
words.s: Visitors expecting a fierce predator were surprised by the docile tiger, which allowed its keepers to examine its teeth without so much as a growl.

words.m: easily managed, controlled, or persuaded
words.s: Once the problem was broken into smaller subproblems, it became tractable, and the team solved in weeks what had defeated them for years.

words.m: inclined to agree or obey; conforming to rules or standards
words.s: The dictator surrounded himself with compliant ministers who never questioned his decrees, and so he learned of the famine only when riots reached the capital.

words.m: to accept or agree reluctantly, without protest
words.s: Unable to muster enough votes to block the merger, the dissenting shareholders chose to acquiesce rather than prolong a costly and unwinnable legal fight.
words.root: Latin ad- + quiescere, 'to rest' (as in quiet)

words.m: open and responsive to suggestion; easily persuaded
words.s: The playwright proved surprisingly amenable to the director's suggestions, rewriting the final act twice without a word of complaint about artistic integrity.
words.root: French amener, 'to lead to': easily led

words.m: easily bent or influenced; yielding to others' wishes
words.s: The regime preferred a pliant press, rewarding editors who softened critical stories and quietly revoking the licenses of those who refused.
words.root: French plier, 'to bend' (as in pliers, ply)

words.m: readily yielding to the authority or will of others
words.s: In the documentary, the younger wolves adopt a submissive posture, lowering their tails and averting their eyes whenever the dominant pair approaches the kill.
words.root: Latin sub- 'under' + mittere 'to send': placing oneself under

words.m: capable of being shaped or influenced; adaptable
words.s: Because young children's beliefs are so malleable, the researchers worried that leading questions might implant memories of events that had never occurred.
words.root: Latin malleus, 'hammer': able to be hammered into shape

words.m: to agree to a demand, request, or proposal, often after resistance
words.s: After weeks of strikes that idled the port, management finally chose to accede to the union's demands for safer equipment and shorter shifts.

words.m: to cease resisting and surrender, especially on agreed terms
words.s: Though the garrison held out for months, starvation finally forced its commander to capitulate, handing over the fortress in exchange for safe passage.
words.root: Latin capitulum, 'heading': surrendering under listed terms

words.m: lying face upward; also, passively failing to act or resist
words.s: Critics charged that the legislature had been supine in the face of executive overreach, rubber-stamping every emergency decree without a single hearing.

words.m: able to be drawn out into wire; easily led or molded
words.s: The cult's leaders sought out ductile recruits, lonely and uncertain young people who would accept any doctrine presented with enough warmth and confidence.
words.root: Latin ducere, 'to lead': easily led or drawn

tc.q: The minister's critics had predicted a fierce confrontation, but when the opposition's demands were finally tabled, she chose to _____, accepting nearly every provision with little more than a perfunctory objection.
tc.why: 'But' reverses the predicted confrontation, and 'accepting nearly every provision with only a perfunctory objection' defines acquiesce. Remonstrate and dissent describe the fight that never came, and temporize (stall) clashes with accepting.

tc.q: Far from being the _____ instrument of the studio executives that early biographers portrayed, the director routinely defied their instructions, reshooting scenes at his own expense when they rejected his cuts.
tc.why: 'Far from' sets the biographers' portrait against the director's actual defiance, so the portrait must be of an easily bent tool: pliant. Maverick and refractory describe the defiant director he actually was.

tc.q: The ethologist cautions against reading the animal's (i) _____ behavior in captivity as evidence of a naturally gentle temperament; in the wild, the same species is notoriously (ii) _____, resisting even the most patient attempts at domestication.
tc.why: Behavior that could be mistaken for a 'gentle temperament' is docile behavior. The semicolon contrasts it with the wild animal, which resists domestication and so is intractable. Tractable is the reversal trap.

tc.q: Although the general had vowed never to (i) _____, the destruction of his supply lines left him little choice; his eventual surrender, however, was anything but (ii) _____, for he wrung from the victors concessions that preserved his army's honor.
tc.why: The vow he broke was a vow never to capitulate, since 'his eventual surrender' follows. A surrender that won honorable concessions was not abject (humiliatingly submissive). 'Negotiated' would contradict the concessions he wrung from the victors.

se.q: Investors had hoped the new chief executive would be _____ to their proposals for restructuring, but she dismissed every one of them within minutes.
se.why: 'But she dismissed every one' contrasts with what investors hoped, which was openness: amenable or receptive. Hostile and averse form a pair describing what actually happened, not what was hoped for.

se.q: The novel's heroine is no _____ ingenue: when her guardian arranges a marriage for her, she flees to the city rather than submit to his will.
se.why: She refuses to 'submit,' so she is no docile or biddable ingenue. Ingenuous and guileless make a pair about innocence, not obedience, and rebellious and willful describe what she actually is.

se.q: Detractors portrayed the regulator as _____, a watchdog that had rolled over for the very industry it was meant to police.
se.why: A watchdog that 'rolled over' is supine or passive. Vigilant and zealous are the opposite of that image, and venal (bribable) is plausible but has no synonym among the choices.

se.q: Because the clay remains _____ only while it is damp, the potter must finish shaping each vessel before the surface begins to harden.
se.why: Clay that must be shaped before it hardens is malleable or pliable while damp. Brittle and friable form a pair that describes clay once it has dried and hardened.

title: Honesty & Candor
rule: This cluster describes truthfulness and moral uprightness: frank speech (candor, forthright, outspoken, unvarnished), innocence of guile (ingenuous, artless, guileless), and principled integrity (probity, rectitude, veracity). The GRE loves the near-miss pairs ingenuous (naively sincere) vs. disingenuous (falsely sincere) and artless (genuine) vs. artful (cunning), and often signals the cluster with contrasts to 'evasive,' 'guarded,' or 'calculated.'
tip: Remember the 'nothing to hide' family: guile-LESS and art-LESS have no trickery in them, and in-GENU-ous (Latin 'freeborn, frank') is not ingenious.

words.m: openness and honesty in expression; frankness
words.s: The memoir's candor about the author's addiction startled readers accustomed to celebrity autobiographies that conceal every failing behind polished anecdotes.
words.root: Latin candor, 'whiteness, brightness' (as in candid, candle)

words.m: direct and outspoken; straightforward in manner
words.s: Unlike his evasive predecessor, the new commissioner gave forthright answers to reporters, admitting plainly that the agency had mishandled the crisis.

words.m: innocently frank and trusting; lacking cunning or worldliness
words.s: Her ingenuous admission that she had never read the book she was reviewing charmed the audience, who had expected the usual pretense of expertise.

words.m: free of deceit or cunning; innocent and sincere
words.s: The swindlers targeted guileless retirees who answered the telephone politely and believed that anyone claiming to be from the bank must be telling the truth.

words.m: without deception or pretension; natural and simple
words.s: The child's artless drawings, made without any training or thought of an audience, possess a directness that many trained painters spend careers trying to recapture.
words.root: Art in its old sense of 'cunning skill' + -less

words.m: truthfulness; conformity to fact or accuracy
words.s: Historians have questioned the veracity of the general's memoirs, noting that several battles he describes in vivid detail occurred while he was on leave.

words.m: strong moral principles; demonstrated honesty and decency
words.s: A judge of unquestioned probity, she recused herself from the case the moment she learned that her former law firm represented one of the parties.
words.root: Latin probus, 'good, honest' (as in prove, probe)

words.m: morally correct behavior or thinking; righteousness
words.s: His unbending rectitude made him an admirable treasurer but a tiresome dinner companion, since he lectured friends about even the smallest ethical lapses.

words.m: plain and straightforward; not embellished or softened
words.s: The inspector's unvarnished report described the hospital's conditions without euphemism, listing every broken ventilator and every unsanitary ward by name.
words.root: Un- + varnish: the truth without its glossy coat

words.m: genuine; not pretended or put on for show
words.s: The scientist's unfeigned delight at being proven wrong impressed her students, who had seen many senior colleagues treat every refutation as a personal insult.

words.m: frank in stating opinions, especially critical or unpopular ones
words.s: An outspoken critic of the dam project, the biologist testified before the legislature even after her university warned that its funding might suffer.
words.root: One who speaks out rather than holding back

words.m: open, honest, and direct in speech or writing
words.s: In a frank assessment that stunned the board, the auditor stated that the company's books had been misleading investors for at least five years.
words.root: Old French franc, 'free'; the Franks were free men

tc.q: The witness's testimony was compelling precisely because it was so _____: she volunteered damaging facts about herself, made no effort to flatter the jury, and admitted when she could not remember.
tc.why: Volunteering damaging facts and admitting lapses of memory describe forthright testimony. Circumspect (cautious) is the trap, since a careful witness would not volunteer damaging facts, and disingenuous is the opposite of what is described.

tc.q: Admirers of the senator praise her _____, pointing out that in four decades of public life, during which many colleagues were indicted for bribery, not a single credible accusation of impropriety has been made against her.
tc.why: The evidence offered (no accusations of impropriety while colleagues took bribes) supports a claim about integrity, which is probity. Acumen and eloquence are virtues too, but the evidence says nothing about them.

tc.q: The narrator appears at first to be thoroughly (i) _____, recounting her misadventures with a childlike openness that invites the reader's trust; only gradually do we realize that this apparent innocence is a carefully constructed pose, and that she is in fact deeply (ii) _____.
tc.why: 'Childlike openness' and 'apparent innocence' define ingenuous. The revealed 'constructed pose' points to the opposite, calculating. Candid and artless would simply repeat the false first impression.

tc.q: Although the official report was dismissed by the ministry as (i) _____, a careful reading shows that its authors were scrupulous about (ii) _____, citing a source for every figure and flagging every claim they could not independently confirm.
tc.why: 'Although' sets a dismissal against the report's real care, so the ministry called it tendentious (biased); meticulous and comprehensive are not dismissive. Citing sources and flagging unconfirmed claims shows care for veracity, not concision or originality.

se.q: Readers accustomed to the guarded prose of most political memoirs will be struck by the author's _____, which extends even to a detailed account of his own worst misjudgments.
se.why: The contrast with 'guarded prose' and the willingness to detail his own misjudgments call for candor or frankness. Reticence and circumspection form a pair that matches the guarded memoirs he is contrasted with, and bombast and grandiloquence are about style, not honesty.

se.q: Though the con artist presented himself as _____, a simple country man bewildered by city ways, his victims later realized that every apparent naivete had been calculated.
se.why: The pose of a 'simple country man' is a guileless or artless persona. Wily and cunning form a pair describing his real nature, but the blank names how he presented himself.

se.q: The committee valued the consultant's _____ assessment precisely because it did not soften bad news to spare anyone's feelings.
se.why: An assessment that does not soften bad news is unvarnished or blunt. Diplomatic and tactful form a pair describing exactly the softening the consultant avoided.

se.q: The biographer argues that the poet's apparent piety was _____, not a mask adopted to placate his devout patrons, citing private letters in which he prays with evident fervor.
se.why: 'Not a mask,' supported by fervent private prayer, means the piety was sincere or unfeigned. Sanctimonious and hypocritical form a pair describing the 'mask' view that the biographer rejects.

title: Deception & Trickery
rule: This cluster covers lying, double-dealing, and clever trickery: false speech (mendacious, prevaricate), concealed motives (duplicity, disingenuous, dissemble, feign), and schemes or the people who run them (chicanery, subterfuge, artifice, charlatan). On the GRE, signals like 'belied,' 'a mask of,' 'professed,' and 'ostensibly' point here, and a classic trap is confusing disingenuous (insincere) with ingenuous (naive).
tip: 'Dis-' flips honesty: disingenuous only pretends to be ingenuous, and dissemble puts on a false likeness (Latin similis, 'like') to hide your real face.

words.m: deceitfulness in speech or conduct; double-dealing
words.s: The spy's duplicity was so complete that even her closest colleagues never suspected she had been passing their secrets to a rival power for decades.

words.m: insincere; falsely pretending to be candid or to know less
words.s: It was disingenuous of the executive to claim ignorance of the defect, since internal emails show he had been briefed on it months earlier.

words.m: not telling the truth; habitually lying
words.s: The tabloid's mendacious account of the trial, invented almost entirely by a reporter who never attended a single session, prompted a successful libel suit.

words.m: the use of trickery to achieve a political, legal, or financial purpose
words.s: Through procedural chicanery, burying key amendments in unrelated bills and scheduling votes at midnight, the faction pushed through measures most legislators had never read.

words.m: deceit used to achieve one's goal or evade something
words.s: Denied a visa, the journalist resorted to subterfuge, entering the country as a member of an agricultural trade delegation in order to report on the famine.
words.root: Latin subter 'beneath' + fugere 'to flee': escaping underneath

words.m: sly or cunning intelligence used to deceive
words.s: Lacking the strength to defeat the giant directly, the hero of the folktale relies on guile, tricking his enemy into revealing the secret of his weakness.
words.root: Old French guile, 'deceit' (related to wile, wily)

words.m: to conceal one's true motives or feelings behind a false appearance
words.s: Though privately furious at being passed over for promotion, she managed to dissemble at the reception, congratulating her rival with apparently heartfelt warmth.

words.m: to speak or act evasively so as to avoid the truth
words.s: When reporters asked about the missing funds, the mayor continued to prevaricate, answering each question with vague references to an ongoing review.

words.m: a person falsely claiming special knowledge or skill; a fraud
words.s: The so-called healer was exposed as a charlatan when investigators discovered that his miraculous tonic consisted of nothing but sugar water and food coloring.

words.m: to deceive or trick someone into believing or doing something
words.s: The forger managed to dupe several eminent art historians, whose confident authentications of his fake Vermeers lent the paintings a credibility they never deserved.
words.root: French dupe, 'hoopoe', a bird thought to be stupid

words.m: clever trickery, or a cunning device used to deceive
words.s: The candidate's folksy manner was pure artifice; aides later revealed that his rumpled jackets and regional slang were chosen by a team of consultants.

words.m: to pretend to have or be affected by a feeling or condition
words.s: To avoid being drafted into the emperor's army, the young prince would feign madness, babbling nonsense whenever recruiting officers visited the palace.
words.root: Latin fingere, 'to shape, invent' (as in fiction)

tc.q: The defendant's apparent cooperation with investigators was, the prosecutor argued, merely a form of _____: while he answered every question politely, he was simultaneously shredding the documents that would have incriminated him.
tc.why: Polite cooperation that hides the shredding of evidence is a deceptive stratagem: subterfuge. Candor and contrition describe what the cooperation only pretended to be.

tc.q: Critics found it _____ for the company to present its new privacy policy as a victory for consumers, since the policy's fine print actually expanded the firm's right to sell customer data.
tc.why: Presenting a self-serving policy as a gift to consumers is falsely sincere: disingenuous. Ingenuous (naively sincere) is the classic look-alike trap and means nearly the opposite.

tc.q: Though rarely (i) _____ in the strict sense, since she seldom states an outright falsehood, the memoirist habitually chooses to (ii) _____ when awkward questions arise, answering so vaguely that readers can never pin her down.
tc.why: Seldom stating 'an outright falsehood' means she is rarely mendacious. Vague answers that cannot be pinned down mean she prevaricates. Elaborate contradicts 'so vaguely,' and candid would contradict the 'though' contrast.

tc.q: The swindler's genius lay not in elaborate (i) _____ but in his acute sense of whom he could (ii) _____: he approached only those whose eagerness to believe in easy riches made deception almost unnecessary.
tc.why: Deception being 'almost unnecessary' contrasts with elaborate trickery, which is artifice. His real talent was choosing whom he could dupe. Placate and indemnify have nothing to do with swindling.

se.q: Long admired as a paragon of integrity, the senator was undone when leaked recordings revealed his breathtaking _____: he had promised each faction whatever it wanted to hear while secretly working against all of them.
se.why: Secretly working against everyone he made promises to is duplicity or perfidy. Probity and rectitude form a pair describing the reputation he lost, and vacillation (wavering) is not the same as deliberate double-dealing.

se.q: Rather than answer the committee's questions directly, the witness chose to _____, offering vague and shifting accounts that committed him to nothing.
se.why: 'Vague and shifting accounts that committed him to nothing' define prevaricate and equivocate. Capitulate and acquiesce form a pair about giving in, and recant (formally retract) has no partner.

se.q: Although the dealer claimed the manuscript was authentic, experts soon dismissed him as a _____ whose 'discoveries' were invariably forgeries.
se.why: Someone who presents forgeries as discoveries is a fraud: charlatan or mountebank. Connoisseur and savant form a pair that means the opposite, and philistine and boor form a pair that insults taste, not honesty.

se.q: The actress was celebrated for her ability to _____ emotions she did not feel, weeping on cue with a conviction that moved even hardened critics.
se.why: Showing 'emotions she did not feel' means she could feign or simulate them. Suppress and stifle form a pair that means hiding real feelings, which is the reverse.

title: Generosity & Benevolence
rule: This cluster describes giving freely and wishing others well: lavish giving (munificent, bountiful, largesse, unstinting), goodwill (benevolent, beneficent, altruistic, philanthropic), and forgiving generosity (magnanimous, clement). The GRE tests fine distinctions (benevolent means wishing good, beneficent means doing good, magnanimous means generous especially toward rivals) and uses 'liberal' in its older sense of 'generous' as a trap.
tip: Latin bene ('well') runs through the cluster: bene-volent wishes well, bene-ficent does well, a bene-factor is the doer, and magn-animous is literally 'great-souled.'

words.m: extremely generous, especially in giving large gifts
words.s: Thanks to a munificent bequest from a former student, the small college was able to build a new library and eliminate tuition for every incoming class.

words.m: generous or forgiving, especially toward a rival or a less powerful person
words.s: In a magnanimous gesture, the victorious candidate invited her bitterest rival to join the cabinet, praising his expertise despite months of personal attacks.

words.m: actively doing good; producing benefits for others
words.s: The foundation's beneficent work in the region, from clinics to wells to schools built over three decades, has measurably lowered infant mortality and raised literacy rates.
words.root: Latin bene 'well' + facere 'to do': doing good

words.m: well-meaning and kindly; disposed to do good
words.s: The orphans remembered the headmistress as a benevolent figure who quietly paid for their books and medicine out of her own modest salary.

words.m: showing selfless concern for the well-being of others
words.s: Some biologists argue that apparently altruistic behavior, such as a bird's warning call that exposes it to predators, ultimately benefits the caller's own genes.

words.m: seeking to promote others' welfare, especially by donating money to good causes
words.s: After selling his company, the founder devoted himself to philanthropic ventures, funding malaria research and endowing scholarships for first-generation college students.

words.m: generous bestowal of gifts or money, often by someone powerful
words.s: The governor's largesse toward his home district, which received new highways, a stadium, and two hospitals, drew accusations that he was buying votes with public money.

words.m: giving generously; also, existing in large, ample quantities
words.s: The village elders were famously bountiful hosts, insisting that every traveler, however poor or unknown, be fed and lodged for as long as needed.

words.m: given or giving without restraint; lavish and wholehearted
words.s: The retiring nurse was honored for her unstinting devotion to her patients, which included countless unpaid night shifts during the epidemic.
words.root: Un- + stint ('to be sparing'): holding nothing back

words.m: giving freely; generous in amount (an older sense the GRE tests)
words.s: The chef is liberal with saffron, using generous pinches in dishes where most cooks, mindful of its cost, would add only a few threads.

words.m: merciful and lenient in judgment; also, mild (of weather)
words.s: Expecting a harsh sentence, the young defendant wept with relief when the clement judge ordered community service instead of prison.

words.m: a person who gives money or help to a person or cause
words.s: The young composer never learned the identity of the anonymous benefactor who paid for her years of study at the conservatory in Vienna.

tc.q: Although the tycoon was notoriously tightfisted in his business dealings, haggling over every invoice, his private charities were remarkably _____, supporting dozens of hospitals and schools on a scale few contemporaries could match.
tc.why: 'Although' sets his stinginess in business against lavish charitable giving on an unmatched scale: munificent. Frugal would repeat the tightfisted side, and ostentatious and clandestine describe how gifts are made, not their generosity.

tc.q: The general's treatment of the defeated rebels was strikingly _____: rather than executing their leaders, as his advisers urged, he pardoned them and restored their confiscated lands.
tc.why: Pardoning instead of executing defines merciful leniency: clement. Vindictive and draconian describe the harsh course his advisers urged and he rejected.

tc.q: Evolutionary theorists long struggled to explain genuinely (i) _____ behavior, since an organism that sacrifices its own reproductive success to aid strangers would seem to be (ii) _____ by natural selection.
tc.why: Sacrificing one's own success to aid strangers is altruistic behavior. It is puzzling because selection should penalize such costs; 'favored' would remove the puzzle the theorists 'struggled to explain.'

tc.q: The museum's patrons were hardly (i) _____, since their gifts had doubled the endowment in a decade, but the curators worried that such (ii) _____ came with strings attached, because several donors expected their own tastes to dictate what the galleries displayed.
tc.why: Donors who doubled the endowment were hardly parsimonious, and 'such' refers back to that generosity: largesse. Austerity is the opposite of what 'such' points back to, and candor is irrelevant to giving.

se.q: Despite his reputation for ruthlessness in the boardroom, the financier was _____ in private, quietly paying the medical bills of employees he had never met.
se.why: 'Despite' a reputation for ruthlessness, he quietly paid strangers' bills, which makes him benevolent or kindly. Callous and pitiless form a pair that repeats his boardroom reputation, and reclusive picks up 'in private' but has no partner.

se.q: The foundation's director insisted that its grants were motivated by purely _____ concerns, though critics noted that each one conveniently burnished the reputation of its corporate sponsor.
se.why: 'Though critics noted' self-serving benefits, the director must have claimed altruistic or selfless motives. Mercenary and venal form a pair describing the critics' suspicion, not the director's claim, and pragmatic has no partner.

se.q: Grateful for the _____ of their patron, the members of the string quartet dedicated their first recording to the heiress who had funded their instruments and rehearsal space.
se.why: Paying for instruments and rehearsal space is generous giving, largesse or munificence. Austerity and parsimony form a pair that means the opposite, and acumen does not explain the quartet's gratitude.

se.q: Victorious in the bitter election, the new prime minister proved surprisingly _____, appointing several of her harshest critics to senior posts.
se.why: Rewarding one's harshest critics after a bitter contest is magnanimous or forgiving behavior. Vindictive and vengeful form a pair that describes the behavior 'surprisingly' says she avoided.

title: Stinginess & Greed
rule: This cluster splits into two related vices: unwillingness to spend or give (parsimonious, miserly, tightfisted, skinflint) and excessive desire to acquire (avaricious, rapacious, covetous, acquisitive, cupidity, venal, mercenary). The GRE often tests connotation (frugal is a virtue, while parsimonious and miserly are faults) and pairs these words against the generosity cluster with contrasts like 'belying his reputation for' or 'hard to reconcile with.'
tip: Cupidity is named for Cupid (desire) but aimed at money, and rapacious shares a root with raptor (rapere, 'to seize'): a bird of prey grabbing everything in reach.

words.m: unwilling to spend money or resources; excessively frugal
words.s: The parsimonious landlord refused to repair the building's broken furnace until tenants, shivering through January, finally reported him to the city's housing inspectors.

words.m: hoarding wealth and spending as little as possible
words.s: Despite his vast fortune, the miserly banker reused envelopes, refused to heat his mansion, and left nothing to the servants who had cared for him.
words.root: Latin miser, 'wretched': the hoarder is miserable

words.m: having extreme greed for wealth or material gain
words.s: The novel's avaricious heirs gather at their dying uncle's bedside not to comfort him but to argue over who will inherit the plantation.

words.m: aggressively greedy or grasping; predatory
words.s: Colonial administrators, rapacious and unaccountable, stripped the province of timber and minerals while leaving its inhabitants without roads, schools, or hospitals.
words.root: Latin rapere, 'to seize' (as in raptor, rapine)

words.m: yearning to possess something, especially what belongs to another
words.s: Neighbors cast covetous glances at the farmer's fertile riverside fields, and several made offers that he politely but firmly declined.
words.root: Old French coveitier, from Latin cupiditas, 'desire'

words.m: intense greed for money or possessions
words.s: The promoters of the scheme counted on their investors' cupidity, knowing that people dazzled by promises of quick riches rarely ask awkward questions.
words.root: Latin cupiditas, 'desire'; Cupid's longing aimed at money

words.m: open to bribery; corruptly motivated by money
words.s: The reformers argued that venal customs officers, who waved through any shipment for a modest bribe, were the smugglers' most valuable allies.

words.m: motivated chiefly by money or personal gain
words.s: His sudden devotion to the elderly widow struck her children as entirely mercenary, especially once they learned he had asked to see her will.
words.root: Latin merces, 'wages': one who works only for pay

words.m: excessively interested in acquiring money or possessions
words.s: An acquisitive collector, she bought entire estates at auction, filling three warehouses with furniture and paintings she rarely bothered to look at.

words.m: sparing and economical with money or food; thrifty (usually positive)
words.s: Raised by frugal parents who mended clothes and grew their own vegetables, she saved enough from a modest salary to retire a decade early.

words.m: a person who spends as little money as possible; a miser
words.s: A notorious skinflint, the old merchant once walked six miles in the rain rather than pay the few pennies a carriage would have cost.
words.root: So cheap he would skin a flint to save it

words.m: unwilling to spend or give money; stingy
words.s: The tightfisted city council funded the new park but refused to pay for maintenance, so within a few years its fountains were dry and its benches broken.
words.root: A fist clenched tight around one's money

tc.q: The critic's portrait of the composer as _____ is hard to reconcile with the archival record, which shows that he quietly paid his impoverished students' rent and gave away most of his royalties.
tc.why: 'Hard to reconcile with' generous acts (paying rent, giving away royalties) means the critic called him stingy: parsimonious. Munificent is the trap, since it agrees with the record instead of conflicting with it.

tc.q: Unlike earlier conquerors, who had been content to collect modest tribute, the new regime was openly _____, seizing farmland, mines, and even household goods to enrich its officials.
tc.why: 'Unlike' the modest earlier conquerors, a regime that seizes everything to enrich itself is rapacious. Magnanimous and ascetic run the opposite way, and indolent contradicts all that active seizing.

tc.q: The economist distinguishes between (i) _____ households, which save prudently out of foresight, and genuinely (ii) _____ ones, which hoard money even at the cost of their own health and comfort.
tc.why: Saving 'prudently out of foresight' defines frugal (positive). Hoarding at the cost of health is the negative extreme, miserly. Provident would repeat the first category instead of distinguishing from it, and indigent means poor, not hoarding.

tc.q: Defenders of the licensing board insisted that its inspectors were merely overworked, not (i) _____; but the investigation revealed a system in which every permit had its price, and in which the inspectors' (ii) _____ was matched only by the developers' eagerness to pay.
tc.why: A system in which 'every permit had its price' shows the inspectors were venal (bribable), the charge the defenders denied. The greed matched by the developers' eagerness to pay is cupidity, while probity is the reverse and lethargy echoes the 'overworked' excuse.

se.q: Investors who had expected the startup's founders to be idealists were dismayed to find them thoroughly _____, willing to abandon the company's mission the moment a larger payout was offered.
se.why: Dropping a mission for a bigger payout shows they were mercenary or venal, driven by money. Quixotic and visionary form a pair matching the idealism investors expected, not what they found.

se.q: The _____ old collector could never be satisfied: no sooner had he acquired one rare manuscript than he began scheming to obtain another.
se.why: An endless hunger to obtain more is acquisitive or avaricious. Frugal and thrifty form a pair about economical spending, the opposite of a compulsive buyer, and jaded contradicts his eagerness.

se.q: Though often mistaken for mere stinginess, the family's _____ habits were born of necessity: having lost everything in the crash, they had learned to waste nothing.
se.why: Habits 'mistaken for stinginess' but actually prudent are frugal or thrifty. Parsimonious and miserly form the trap pair, since they name the stinginess the sentence says was a misreading.

se.q: Medieval moralists reserved special scorn for the _____, who hoarded gold in locked chests while beggars starved at his gate.
se.why: Hoarding gold while beggars starve describes a skinflint or miser. Spendthrift and prodigal form a pair naming the opposite vice, and an ascetic renounces wealth instead of hoarding it.
